front.title: The Base64 Data Encodings: base64 and base64url

abstract.t: A profile of RFC 4648 for nish/crypto/base64url and nish/base64: base 64 encoding with the standard alphabet and padding (Section 4), and with the URL and filename safe alphabet and no padding (Section 5). It quotes RFC 4648, the main source; every binding sentence of RFC 4648 (MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, REQUIRED) is tested or excluded here. The base 32 and base 16 encodings are not implemented and not profiled.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

nish/crypto/base64url exports a strict codec for each base 64 alphabet. The standard one (base64StdPad*) writes padding and reads only canonical text: a length that is a multiple of four, padding only as the last one or two characters, and zero pad bits. The URL one (base64url*) writes no padding, as the specifications that use it (JWS, JWK) state, and reads only canonical unpadded text: no = anywhere, no length of 1 modulo 4, and zero pad bits. Every decoder returns null (or -1, for base64StdPadDecodedLength) where it refuses.

nish/base64 is an encoder only, with the standard alphabet and padding. Its functions are declared after a second module line, as reference functions, so each clause that tests one also calls a function of nish/crypto/base64url: each is held equal to the strict encoder on every sample.

Section 10 prints test vectors for the standard alphabet only; the URL and filename safe alphabet has none. The vector rows hold the standard encoder and decoder to Section 10, and the properties hold the URL codec to the standard one: the URL encoding of any bytes is their standard encoding with + and / written as - and _ and the padding dropped.

section.name: Line Feeds and Padding

blockquote.t: Implementations MUST NOT add line feeds to base-encoded data unless the specification referring to this document explicitly directs base encoders to add line feeds after a specific number of characters.
Implementations MUST include appropriate pad characters at the end of encoded data unless the specification referring to this document explicitly states otherwise.

section.name: Non-Alphabet Characters

blockquote.t: Implementations MUST reject the encoded data if it contains characters outside the base alphabet when interpreting base-encoded data, unless the specification referring to this document explicitly states otherwise.

section.name: Canonical Encoding

blockquote.t: These pad bits MUST be set to zero by conforming encoders, which is described in the descriptions on padding below.
In some environments, the alteration is critical and therefore decoders MAY chose to reject an encoding if the pad bits have not been set to zero.

section.name: Base 64 Encoding

blockquote.t: The encoding process represents 24-bit groups of input bits as output strings of 4 encoded characters.
Each 6-bit group is used as an index into an array of 64 printable characters.
Padding at the end of the data is performed using the '=' character.

front.title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

abstract.t: This document describes the commonly used base 64, base 32, and base 16 encoding schemes. It also discusses the use of line-feeds in encoded data, use of padding in encoded data, use of non-alphabet characters in encoded data, use of different encoding alphabets, and canonical encodings. front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
